h1: What investors ask a brewery founder
title: What Investors Ask a Brewery Founder | Craft Beer School
desc: The questions investors and lenders ask a brewery founder: market, unit economics, working capital, team, licences and risk. How to answer them.
teaser: Investors rarely ask about your recipe first. They ask how you make money, how long it takes and what could go wrong.
standfirst: A brewery pitch is judged on numbers, people and risk. Prepare for these questions and you will answer with figures, not adjectives.
sections: Who is the customer and how many?

Investors want to know who buys your beer, where, how often and why they choose you. Be specific: taproom visitors, bars, shops, online customers. Show how you know, with sales from a test, a pilot or a waiting list. A claim about the number of beer drinkers in the country says little.

Be ready to explain your competition: other local brewers, imports and mainstream lager. Say what you do differently, plainly.

Show proof of demand in whatever form you have. Preorders, letters of intent from venues, taproom sales from pop-ups and contract brews that sold out all carry weight. A single enthusiastic friend does not.

Investors also ask how big the market can get. Answer with a reasoned local estimate based on population, venues and drinking habits. Avoid headline numbers copied from reports you cannot check.
What does a litre cost and sell for?

Show the cost per litre of beer, packaged or served, next to the price you will get. Break it into ingredients, labour, energy, packaging, duty and overhead. Show the margin. Lenders often probe whether your price is realistic for the market. See pricing a pint in a brewpub.

Avoid single figures with no workings. A sheet that anyone can check beats a headline number.

Show the sensitivity too. What happens to margin if malt costs rise, if volume is lower than planned or if the price has to drop? A founder who has tested the numbers shows control. Include working capital: how many days between spending on ingredients and receiving payment.

Know your break-even volume: the litres you must sell each month for revenue to cover all costs. Investors will ask for it. A founder who can state it and explain how long it takes to reach gains credibility at once.
How much money and what for?

List how much you need and what it pays for: equipment, site works, licences, stock, staff and working capital. Show the timing. Investors prefer a plan that includes a reserve. See start-up costs founders forget for lines founders miss.

Say how the money will be repaid or how an equity investor might exit. Be honest that a small brewery may not offer a quick sale.

Explain staged spending. You may not need all the money at once. Investors like to see milestones that release funds, such as licences secured, the plant commissioned or a sales target reached.

Explain why a brewpub, a production brewery or contract brewing is right for you and what you will do if it does not work. Read brewpub or production brewery to prepare. Investors like founders who have compared the options.

Show that you can change course. Many breweries begin as one thing and become another, adding a taproom, packaged beer or non-alcoholic lines. Show which options you have kept open.

Explain how the plan changes if the first year runs at half the volume. A fallback, such as a contract brew or a smaller team, reassures a cautious backer.

People are the biggest risk. Explain who brews, who sells and who manages the money. Say what experience each brings. If there is a gap, say how you will fill it. A founder without brewing experience should show a head brewer or adviser. See writing a head brewer job description.

Mention advisers, mentors and the support you have. An experienced brewer, accountant or lawyer on your side lowers risk. Say what they do and how they are paid.
Licences, risks and what you track

Show where you are in the licensing chain and what could delay it. Name your main risks: supply, cash, quality, regulation and staff. Then give your plan for each. Say which numbers you will report each month, such as volume, price, margin and cash.

Do not promise returns you cannot support. A cautious, well-argued plan is more convincing than a bold one with gaps.

Be ready for the question of what you will do if the licence is late or refused. A thoughtful answer, with the lease terms and the cash needed to wait, shows you have thought it through. Read brewery licensing: the steps most countries share before the meeting.
faqs: Do investors want to taste the beer?
Often yes, but they weigh the business more. Bring beer that represents what you will sell. Be ready to explain how you will keep it consistent.
How much should I borrow or raise?
Enough to cover costs, a reserve and the time to reach sales. Build the figure from a detailed sheet. Have it checked by an adviser.
What if I have no brewing experience?
Show how you will cover it: an experienced head brewer, a consultant or a partner. Investors look for gaps and for plans to fill them.
